config.title: Discriminated Union Props

intro.title: Discriminated Union Props
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Angular component that displays different types of notifications, such as success, warning, and error messages. You will learn how to use a TypeScript feature called a discriminated union to define the component's input property, ensuring that each notification type has a specific shape. This involves creating a union type with a common 'type' property that acts as a discriminator, and then using Angular's @Input decorator to pass this data into your component. By the end, you'll understand how discriminated unions make your component's props type-safe and easier to manage.
intro.usecase: Discriminated union props are essential in Angular applications where components need to handle multiple distinct states or variants. You'll see this pattern in dashboard widgets that can display as charts, tables, or summary cards—each requiring different data and rendering logic. Form components often use discriminated unions to handle different input types like text fields, dropdowns, or date pickers with type-safe validation. Notification systems implement this pattern to manage different alert types (success, warning, error) with distinct styling and behavior. This approach ensures type safety while reducing conditional complexity in your component templates.

objectives: Construct a discriminated union type in TypeScript to define component props.
Apply the discriminated union type as the input property interface for an Angular component.
Implement conditional rendering in the component template based on the discriminator property.
Configure the component to accept and validate props using the discriminated union structure.
Bind different data structures to the component instance based on the discriminator value.
Manipulate component logic to handle the distinct cases of the union type appropriately.

steps.title: Import Component and CommonModule from @angular/core
steps.instruction: Import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common' to create the component and enable basic directives.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to import multiple symbols from their respective packages.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component file will have the necessary imports to create an Angular component with basic template directives.
successCriteria: Component is imported from '@angular/core' and CommonModule is imported from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both Component and CommonModule from their correct packages.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the import statements. You need to import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.

steps.title: Create the main component class with selector and template
steps.instruction: Create the main component class named DiscriminatedUnionComponent with selector 'app-discriminated-union' and an empty inline template.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator with selector and template properties. The template can be an empty string for now.
steps.seedCode:
import { Component, CommonModule } from '@angular/core';

// Create the DiscriminatedUnionComponent class here
steps.expectedOutcome: A component class is defined with the correct selector and an empty template.
successCriteria: The DiscriminatedUnionComponent class is created with @Component decorator containing selector: 'app-discriminated-union' and template: ''.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have both the selector set to 'app-discriminated-union' and an empty template string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component class wasn't created correctly. Check that you're using @Component decorator with the specified selector and template.

steps.title: Define discriminated union types for props
steps.instruction: Inside the DiscriminatedUnionComponent class, define two TypeScript interfaces: TextContent with properties 'type' (string literal 'text') and 'text' (string), and ImageContent with properties 'type' (string literal 'image'), 'src' (string), and 'alt' (string).
steps.hint: Use the 'type' property with literal string values ('text'/'image') as the discriminant. The union type can be defined as 'type Content = TextContent | ImageContent;'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have three type definitions: TextContent, ImageContent, and Content union, enabling type-safe discriminated union props.
successCriteria: TextContent interface has 'type: "text"' and 'text: string', ImageContent interface has 'type: "image"', 'src: string', and 'alt: string', and Content is a union of both interfaces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Check that both interfaces have a 'type' property with literal string values ('text'/'image') and that Content is a union of both.
steps.feedbackWrong: The types aren't defined correctly. Review the structure of discriminated unions: each interface needs a distinct 'type' literal and Content should combine them with '|'.

steps.title: create a union type Content that combines bot
steps.instruction: create a union type Content that combines both interfaces.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' property with literal string values ('text'/'image') as the discriminant. The union type can be defined as 'type Content = TextContent | ImageContent;'.
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Create template with ngIf to check union type
steps.instruction: In the component's template, add a <div> with *ngIf to check if content.type is 'text' and display the text content.
steps.hint: Use Angular's *ngIf structural directive with a condition like content.type === 'text'. Inside the div, you can display the text property from the content object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will conditionally render text content when content.type is 'text'.
successCriteria: The template includes a <div> with *ngIf checking content.type === 'text' and displays the text property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the *ngIf condition checks content.type === 'text' and displays the text property inside the div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't yet have the required conditional rendering. Add a <div> with *ngIf to check if content.type is 'text' and display the text content.

steps.title: Add else block for image content display
steps.instruction: In the component's template, add an else block to the existing ngIf to handle when content.type is 'image' and display the image content.
steps.hint: Use Angular's *ngIf else syntax to show different content based on the discriminated union type.

steps.expectedOutcome: The template now has an else block that will display image content when content.type is 'image'.
successCriteria: The template contains an *ngIf with an else clause that handles the image case and displays the image properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added the else block correctly with the ng-template reference.
steps.feedbackWrong: The else block for image content is missing or incorrect. Review Angular's *ngIf else syntax.

steps.title: Create method to toggle between union types
steps.instruction: In the DiscriminatedUnionComponent class, add a method named toggleContent that switches the content property between a TextContent object and an ImageContent object.
steps.hint: The method should assign a new object to this.content. Use the type property to determine which case to switch to.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a toggleContent method that can switch the content property between the two discriminated union cases.
successCriteria: The DiscriminatedUnionComponent class contains a toggleContent method that correctly assigns either a TextContent or ImageContent object to this.content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a method, but it doesn't fully switch between the union types. Make sure it properly assigns both TextContent and ImageContent objects.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggleContent method is missing or doesn't switch between the discriminated union types. Review the method implementation.

steps.title: Add button to trigger type switching
steps.instruction: Add a button element to your component's template with a click event bound to the toggleContent() method. Place it after the existing conditional blocks.
steps.hint: Use Angular's event binding syntax (click)="methodName()" to connect the button click to your toggle method.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button with click handler
<button (click)="handleClick()">Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will include a button that, when clicked, calls the toggleContent() method to switch between text and image content types.
successCriteria: A button element with (click)="toggleContent()" event binding is added to the template after the conditional blocks.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but make sure it has the correct click event binding to toggleContent().
steps.feedbackWrong: The button with click event binding is missing or incorrect. Check that you've added <button (click)="toggleContent()"> with proper syntax.

steps.title: Add CSS classes for visual distinction
steps.instruction: Add a CSS class to the text content div and a different CSS class to the image content div in your template.
steps.hint: Use the class attribute on the div elements. You can name them something like 'text-content' and 'image-content'.

successCriteria: Both div elements in the template have class attributes with distinct class names.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a class to one div, but both content type divs need their own CSS classes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template divs don't have CSS classes yet. Add class attributes to both the text and image content divs.

steps.title: Test the discriminated union behavior
steps.instruction: Run the application and click the toggle button to see the type-safe switching between text and image content.
steps.hint: Use the Angular CLI command 'ng serve' to start the development server, then open your browser to see the component. Click the button to toggle between the two content types.

steps.expectedOutcome: The application runs successfully and displays either text or image content based on the discriminated union type. Clicking the toggle button switches between the two content types without errors.
successCriteria: The application runs without errors and clicking the toggle button correctly switches between text and image content display.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: The application runs but there might be issues with the toggle functionality. Check that the button click properly triggers the type switching.
